stories.title: Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis
stories.summary: Also on Friday, the Pope phoned Russian President Vladimir Putin from hospital to urge a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where access to food and water has been cut off for thousands. "The fact that he accepted the call and spoke with the Pope may, I hope, be a sign that the Pope's request will indeed be carried out," said Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican's secretary of state. Without mentioning a ceasefire, the Kremlin said: "The Vatican's intention to help create the conditions necessary to ensure the safety of the town's population and to organise vital supplies has been supported".

stories.title: Power plant attacks reflect Russian blueprint to make Ukrainian cities unlivable
stories.summary: As Russian missiles and drones have systematically slammed into power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the rolling blackouts and water outages have increasingly resembled a supposed Russian blueprint to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities seen by the Guardian. Even as Donald Trump unilaterally declared an “energy ceasefire” last week between Moscow and Kyiv, Russia continued with its methodical and devastating strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, in particular in Kyiv, in a strategy meant to punish Ukraine’s population and drive the country to capitulation.

stories.title: USC scientists discover how to create a never-ending supply of cancer-fighting cells
stories.summary: Scientists at the University of Southern California (USC) have discovered a way to produce a potentially renewable supply of cancer-fighting immune cells, opening a promising new direction for cancer treatment. By working with immature cells that can develop into powerful immune defenders, the researchers have created a system capable of generating large numbers of genetically engineered cells that recognize tumors and help activate the body's natural defenses. The breakthrough, described in a study published in Cell, could help overcome some of the biggest obstacles facing cancer immunotherapy, including the difficulty of manufacturing enough immune cells and keeping them active in the body.
stories.displayTitle: USC scientists discover how to create a never-ending supply of cancer-fighting cells
stories.originalSummary: USC scientists have discovered a way to create a potentially renewable supply of genetically engineered immune cells that can attack cancer and strengthen the body's natural defenses. By growing and modifying immature immune cells rather than mature ones, researchers developed a system that can continuously produce tumor-fighting cells inside the body.

stories.title: A highway instead of a racetrack: Strong coupling of light and sound in an optical fiber
stories.summary: For the first time, scientists have achieved strong coupling between light and long-lived acoustic vibrations in an optical fiber. Optical fibers are used in both classical telecommunications and quantum communication and could serve not only as connections between computing nodes but also as quantum processors themselves in the future. The results, published in Nature Physics, pave the way for new technologies in quantum signal processing. Mechanical and acoustic vibrations can be used to convert signals across various frequency ranges, from optical frequencies (terahertz) to microwaves (gigahertz) and even lower frequencies (megahertz or kilohertz). For instance, this capability is essential to connect multiple quantum computers operating at gigahertz frequencies via optical links.

stories.title: Mysterious 'Golden Tree' Coral Is So Weird, Scientists Had to Create a New Family on The Tree of Life
stories.summary: The newly discovered coral lives in strange conditions that seem inhospitable to life. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute/Breedy et al., ZooKeys, 2026) In the twilight deeps of the Eastern Pacific Ocean, a magical sight can be found on a seamount off the coast of Costa Rica. As the underwater vehicle SuBastian glides over a rocky outcrop oddly coated with a fuzzy pink patina and punctuated with basket-shaped gleaming white sponges, a majestic yellow form emerges from the darkness. It looks like a golden tree, so vividly yellow you can imagine it glowing. Then, as the camera zooms closer, you can see the pink fuzz moving – a thick carpet of stars from which the golden tree blooms.

reserveStories.title: Google's Quantum Computer Just Achieved a Major Breakthrough With 'Magic States'
reserveStories.summary: Quantum computers have an inconvenient problem: they're magnificently efficient at making mistakes. These marvelous machines could one day solve problems that would bring even the most powerful conventional supercomputers to their knees. But the quantum states behind their incredible computing power are also exceptionally fragile, and keeping errors under control is a monumental task. In fact, a fully functional quantum computer could end up devoting most of its resources not to performing calculations, but simply to making sure those calculations are correct. Now, the wizards at Google have demonstrated a new way to make quantum computing significantly less error-prone, using a technique with the delightfully appropriate name "magic state cultivation".

reserveStories.title: Norman McCubbin obituary
reserveStories.summary: My brother Norman McCubbin, who has died aged 77, was a scientist who worked at the forefront of experimental particle physics. A leading light in experiments that took place on the Large Hadron Collider, the world’s biggest and most powerful particle accelerator at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (Cern) in Switzerland, he spent the last five years of his working life as director of the particle physics department at the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory (RAL) in Oxfordshire, until his retirement in 2012. Afterwards he became a tutor to undergraduates at St Anne’s College, Oxford, and was still in that role at his death.

reserveStories.title: Millions of Americans Use Cannabis to Help Them Sleep. It Could Be Doing The Opposite.
reserveStories.summary: An estimated 22 million Americans currently use cannabis as a form of sleep aid, and almost one in four says they're likely to try the drug to help them sleep. But despite the widespread view that cannabis can help you get a good night's rest, the evidence is starting to suggest otherwise. In recent years, scientists have linked cannabis to sleep disruption, and reviews have suggested that the drug may in fact have an overall detrimental effect on sleep quality, despite what many users might think it's doing for them. A new study in JAMA Network Open highlights this paradox, suggesting a possible disconnect between the sleep quality of cannabis users and their own perception of how well they're sleeping.

reserveStories.title: NASA to Help Unlock Mysteries of Mars’ Moons in Upcoming Mission
reserveStories.summary: NASA is playing an important role in JAXA’s (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) MMX (Martian Moons eXploration) mission, to advance our understanding of Mars’ moons and build on the agency’s long history of exploring the Red Planet. The mission aims to characterize and determine the origin of Mars’ moons Phobos and Deimos and deliver a sample of Phobos to Earth. The MMX spacecraft is targeting launch from JAXA’s Tanegashima Space Center in Japan at 3:41 p.m. EDT on Monday, Oct. 19 (4:41 a.m. JST on Tuesday, Oct. 20).

reserveStories.title: AI model decodes the language cells use to communicate
reserveStories.summary: As an embryo develops from a small cluster of stem cells, those once “blank slate” cells begin to take on more specialized roles like brain, liver, or muscle cells, and organize themselves into three-dimensional structures such as tissues and organs. The fate of each cell — what type of specialized cell it will become — depends on which genes are turned on or off in the cell. These patterns of gene activity shape the cell’s structure and function, enabling it to take on a specific role in the body. But this decision isn’t up to individual cells.

reserveStories.originalSummary: A new computational approach reveals how cells communicate to assemble into tissues. This could accelerate stem cell engineering, improve disease models, and inform therapies.

reserveStories.title: Pakistan school roof collapse kills at least 34 children and teacher
reserveStories.summary: At least 34 schoolchildren and a female teacher have died after the roof of a school collapsed during morning classes in the northern Pakistani city ⁠of Peshawar. As panicked parents ​and relatives thronged the site of the privately run al-Khair school to search for their loved ones, rescue workers spent hours pulling children from the rubble. Most of the victims were under 13 years old ⁠and from low-income households. At least 45 children suffered injuries, ranging from minor wounds to severe trauma, said Arif Khattak, the regional director of emergency services. As panicked parents ​and relatives thronged the site of the privately run al-Khair school to search for their loved ones, rescue workers spent hours pulling children from the rubble. reserveStories.title: Indonesia fights fire with dry ice as toxic haze spreads across region
reserveStories.summary: As fires ravage Indonesia, emitting a toxic smoke that has drawn the ire of regional neighbours, the government is testing an unusual new approach to tackle the haze: dry ice. Having tried cloud seeding, water bombing and sending in army personnel to fight the fires, Indonesia’s coordinating security minister said dry ice would be dropped on the province of South Sumatra on Thursday. “This trial of dry ice dispersal is being conducted under the president’s direct instruction to help tackle the haze in South Sumatra,” minister Dudung Abdurachman was quoted as saying by state news agency Antara.

reserveStories.title: Can extra weight weigh on your dog's brain?
reserveStories.summary: Scientists have learned a lot about what happens to the human body as we age. But there's still much to learn about how other species age, including dogs. Even carrying extra weight could affect a dog's cognitive health. Alexandra Genualdi, a student at Oklahoma State University who presented her research in September at the American Physiological Society's 2026 Comparative Physiology conference in Orlando, talks about her efforts to learn more. What is your research trying to uncover? We wanted to understand whether carrying extra body weight affects the health and well-being of canine companion animals, specifically golden retrievers.

reserveStories.title: New DNA sequencing methods detect rare mutations acquired as bodies grow and age
reserveStories.summary: Somatic mutations, the DNA changes that occur as our bodies grow and age, not only hold an important key to cancer but are emerging as the seeds of a wide range of common, noncancerous diseases. The Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network, a National Institutes of Health Common Fund initiative to catalog all the normal processes of somatic mutation, has published its first comprehensive benchmarking study in the journal Cell. The researchers developed and calibrated new sequencing technologies, experimental approaches and computational methods that now make it possible to detect different types of somatic mutations with greater sensitivity and specificity than ever before.

reserveStories.title: Scientists discover how harmful “zombie cells” hide from the immune system
reserveStories.summary: Researchers led by Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University have discovered a protein that may allow harmful aging cells to escape detection by the immune system. By helping these cells remain in the body instead of being cleared away, the protein could contribute to their accumulation and the development of health problems associated with aging. The discovery, published in Cell Metabolism, identifies PD-L2 as a potential target for therapies aimed at eliminating harmful aging cells. Scientists also believe the protein could serve as a blood marker, providing a way to detect and monitor these cells.

reserveStories.originalSummary: Scientists have discovered a protein that may help harmful aging cells hide from the immune system, allowing them to accumulate and fuel age-related health problems. reserveStories.title: Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses
reserveStories.summary: The White House’s unilateral effort to negotiate an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has collapsed as Moscow sent a record swarm of drones overnight to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine and Kyiv appeared to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries despite warnings from Donald Trump. Moscow accused Ukraine of launching a strike against a Russian oil refinery in the Ryazan region, its first since Trump abruptly declared an “energy ceasefire” that neither Russia nor Ukraine said they had agreed to. Trump has demanded that Volodymyr Zelenskyy stop attacking Russian oil refineries, claiming it is the cause of a global rise in the price of diesel fuel.

reserveStories.title: Albania’s prime minister vows not to resign over student-led protests
reserveStories.summary: Albania’s prime minister has said he will not resign as a protest movement, initially prompted by a proposal to build a Trump family-backed resort in the Balkan state, turned violent with clashes convulsing the capital for a third consecutive day. Speaking on Thursday after calls by students who this week assumed control of the anti-government demonstrations that have rattled Tirana since June, Edi Rama said: “Governments are changed through democratic elections. We had elections last year, not a revolution.” Rama’s comments to Reuters came hours before fresh clashes erupted outside the education ministry, where riot police responded to rock-throwing youths with teargas and water cannon.

reserveStories.title: Ancient Hole in Neanderthal Shoulder Blade May Be The Oldest Spear Attack Ever Discovered
reserveStories.summary: The left scapula of Shanidar A. (University of Cambridge) When the end came, it must have been very painful. In a moment of violence roughly 75,000 years ago, something sharp pierced the body of the victim, known only as Shanidar A, an adult Neanderthal estimated to be 45 years old. The deadly injury left a gaping 15-millimeter-wide hole in Shanidar A's left shoulder blade. We can't say for sure what made that hole, but in a new study in Scientific Reports, researchers suggest it was probably a spear, meaning this could be the earliest known example of an interpersonal spear attack in the hominin fossil record.

reserveStories.title: America's historic preservation law is in peril, advocates say. Here's what's at stake
reserveStories.summary: It's been exactly 60 years since President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) into law, alongside half a dozen conservation bills. "We have come here this morning to give part of our country back to its people," Johnson declared at the bill signing on Oct. 15, 1966. Now, historic preservation advocates say, the government is trying to yank the public's power away. "Preservation, from its inception, has worked best with public and private partnership," Brent Leggs, the president and CEO of the nonprofit National Trust for Historic Preservation, told NPR. "Over the last year and a half, the federal government has divested that responsibility."

reserveStories.title: Satellite data reveal how Antarctica’s ice cliffs behave over time
reserveStories.summary: With rising temperatures, the buttressing ice shelves at the edges the Antarctic ice sheet are melting and calving off at record rates, leaving behind sheer cliffs of solid ice. The stability of these exposed ice cliffs could influence how Antarctica further breaks apart and contributes to sea level rise around the world. Scientists have assumed that an ice cliff’s stability depends on its height: Ice cliffs that are taller than 100 meters — about the height of the Statue of Liberty — should collapse under their own weight. And once a cliff sloughs off, it should expose even taller, inland cliffs that collapse in turn.

reserveStories.originalSummary: The cliffs don’t always collapse in the runaway process that scientists had expected.

reserveStories.title: Laser pulses bring order to a quantum material's tiny electrical regions
reserveStories.summary: Physicists at Auburn University have used flashes of laser light to bring order to tiny electrically charged "islands" inside a crystal. The discovery helps answer a decades-old question about how the material organizes itself and shows how light could be used to control its behavior—a step toward exploring new technologies for processing and storing information. The research was led by Wencan Jin, the Thomas and Jean Walter endowed associate professor in Auburn's Department of Physics, and graduate student Mohamed Kandil. Their study, "Optical Poling of a Quantum Ferroelectric Metal across the Order-Disorder Phase Transition," was selected as an Editors' Suggestion in Physical Review Letters.

reserveStories.title: Quantum calculations reveal how spin defects lose energy
reserveStories.summary: When light hits a tiny defect embedded in a solid material like diamond or silicon carbide, it can kick the defect's electrons into an excited state. These spin defects have the potential to be used as stable, readable qubits for quantum technologies, for example, quantum sensing. But modeling the full physics of their energetics over time—a key step in developing spin defects into new technologies—is a challenging task. Now, researchers at the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME) have built a computational framework that captures the full optical cycle of such spin defects, including the prediction of internal conversion, a process particularly hard to model.

reserveStories.title: A fungus is threatening the world’s food supply. Scientists just found a new defense
reserveStories.summary: Scientists have uncovered a promising new way to protect some of the world's most important food crops from a destructive fungus that threatens global food security. By engineering the natural immune defenses of plants, researchers have developed an experimental approach that could eventually help wheat, rice, and barley resist fungal infections more effectively. The international research team, led by scientists at the John Innes Centre in the United Kingdom, investigated a recently discovered group of plant immune receptors. They identified how these proteins recognize invading pathogens and demonstrated that they can be modified to detect multiple fungal threats.
reserveStories.displayTitle: A fungus is threatening the world’s food supply. Scientists just found a new defense
reserveStories.originalSummary: Scientists have discovered a potential new weapon against a devastating fungus that threatens rice, wheat, and barley worldwide. By engineering a special type of plant immune receptor, researchers created defenses capable of recognizing multiple fungal threats at once. The breakthrough could eventually lead to crops with powerful, long-lasting disease resistance, helping protect a global food supply increasingly threatened by spreading infections and climate change.

reserveStories.title: Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills two, minister says
reserveStories.summary: Two security personnel have been killed in a Houthi missile attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city of Aden in southern Yemen, which is the seat of the internationally-recognised government, officials say. Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani told the BBC that the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when five ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace, but that many others were injured. The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said they struck "the Saudi enemy's military operations headquarters in Aden". A coalition led by Saudi Arabia backs the government and is providing air support for an offensive by pro-government forces against the Iran-backed Houthis.

reserveStories.title: Healthy Coral Reversed Bleaching in Its Neighbor With Just 1 Week of Contact
reserveStories.summary: Corals cannot survive long without the algae that live inside their bodies. But under stress from factors like heat, pollution, and UV exposure, these algae can become toxic to the coral, which evicts them. Without their algal symbionts, corals turn white, in what is known as coral bleaching. A 'bleached' coral has limited time to acquire new algal symbionts before it starves to death. With the threat of coral bleaching events growing each year, Stanford scientists have found a technique that could help rescue corals on the brink of death. "While bleached corals may be dying, they are not dead yet," says Stanford marine scientist Danny Collins.
